newsitem.title: USA: Dole threatens to go after Clinton ethics.
newsitem.headline: Dole threatens to go after Clinton ethics.

text.p: By Alan Elsner, U.S. Political Correspondent
Republican candidate Bob Dole on Monday threatened to attack the ethics of the Clinton administration in the final presidential debate in a bid to close a yawning gap in public opinion polls.

Dole, campaigning in Kansas City, Missouri, two days ahead of the debate, seized on the latest ethical questions to hit the administration concerning campaign contributions to Clinton from Asian businessmen.
"There are a whole lot of problems here that have been raised. Taking money from a foreign nation. They gave it back when somebody caught them, but why did they do it?" he said.
He said the affair raised questions about whether the contributions persuaded the United States to take a soft line against human rights abuses by Indonesia in the annexed territory of East Timor.
"We're going to raise the questions every day until the president's properly responded," Dole declared.

Apparently listening to advisers urging him to hit the character issue harder, Dole said about 30 members of Clinton's administration "are already gone -- they are in jail or they are indicted or they are out of there."
"Then he talks about an ethical administration," Dole said. "Well he does not have an ethical administration and we're going to go after him on that on Wednesday night."

The fundraising affair involves an Indonesian couple's $425,000 contribution to the Democratic Party and another donation from a South Korean company that the party returned after media queries about it.

It seemed unlikely at first glance to derail Clinton's seemingly irresistible progress towards an election victory on Nov 5. The latest Reuters tracking poll showed Clinton lengthening his lead every day for the past six days. He now leads Dole by 14.8 percentage points.
Clinton, in New Mexico to prepare for the debate with Dole on Wednesday night in San Diego, has declined to respond in detail to charges of influence peddling to foreigners.

Looking ahead to the debate, he said: "Senator Dole will decide his strategy and I will decide mine and we'll see what the people have to say afterwards. The most important thing, I hope, is that it will be something people will feel better about when it's over."
Clinton's aides said the Republicans were desperate, realising they were on the verge of defeat.

Several Republican lawmakers have suggested it may be necessary to appoint an independent counsel to investigate whether the Democratic Party received illegal foreign contributions. This includes nearly $1 million from individuals tied to an Indonesian financial conglomerate, the Lippo Group.

Clinton's ties to Indonesian billionaire James Riady have been fiercely attacked by Republicans, who say the wealthy Indonesian has exerted influence over the president by contributing to his political causes and his inauguration.
Attention has focused particularly on John Huang, a former vice chairman of Lippo's California banking subsidiary who moved on to become vice finance chairman of the Democratic National Committee.

Newsweek magazine reports this week that Huang "has raised millions from Asian sources" for Clinton's re-election effort, including a gift of $425,000 from Arief Wiriandinata, the son- in-law of a major investor in Riady's Lippo Group.

The DNC was forced to return a $250,000 contribution solicited by Huang after checking into questions posed by the Los Angeles Times and finding the contribution came from a South Korean company. Vice President Al Gore said on Sunday it was not unusual for political parties to return contributions.
